{{Short description|American theoretical and computational chemist}}
'''Kim K. Baldridge''' is an American theoretical and computational chemist who works to develop quantum mechanical methodologies and apply quantum chemical methods to problems in life sciences, materials science, and general studies. She is professor and vice dean in the School of Pharmaceutical Science and Technology of [[Tianjin University]] in China, where she also directs the High Performance Computing Center.<ref name=cd/>

==Education and career==
Baldridge is originally from [[Minot, North Dakota]], and graduated from [[Minot State University]] in 1982.<ref name=minot>{{cite web|url=https://www.minotstateu.edu/pio/docs/inside/2013/2013_09_25.pdf|title=MSU Academic Hall of Fame honors Kim Baldridge|work=Public Information Office Newsletter|publisher=[[Minot State University]]|date=September 25, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150906005745/https://www.minotstateu.edu/pio/docs/inside/2013/2013_09_25.pdf |archive-date=September 6, 2015}}</ref> She earned her Ph.D. in 1988 from [[North Dakota State University]] working under the supervision of Mark S. Gordon, and was a postdoctoral researcher at [[Wesleyan University]] until 1994.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://spstmeeting.tju.edu.cn/oneschool/Front/bio/393 |title=Kim Baldridge |website=[[Tianjin University]] School of Pharmaceutical Science and Technology |access-date=May 29, 2024 }}</ref> After becoming a scientist at the [[San Diego Supercomputer Center]], she became a visiting professor at the [[University of California, San Diego]] in 1995,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sdsc.edu/News%20Items/PR103095.html|title=SDSC Chemist Awarded Visiting Professorships for Women Grant by the NSF|publisher=San Diego Supercomputer Center|date=October 30, 1995|accessdate=2020-10-27}}</ref> and continued to work at the San Diego Supercomputer Center and hold an adjunct professorship at the university<ref name=UCSD2001>{{cite web|url=https://biology.ucsd.edu/about/news/article_051601.html|title=UCSD Professors in the Biology and Physical Sciences Divisions Honored for Achievements|date=May 16, 2001 |first1=Brett |last1=Howell |first2=Kim |last2=McDonald |publisher=[[University of California, San Diego]] |accessdate=2020-10-27 }}</ref> before becoming a professor of theoretical chemistry at the [[University of Zurich]] in Switzerland in 2004.<ref name=minot/><ref>{{cite web |url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/82/i8/ZURICH-PULLS-CHEMICAL-TALENT.html |title=Zurich Pulls in Chemical Talent |last=Rouhi |first=Maureen A. |date=February 3, 2004 |website=[[Chemical & Engineering News|C&EN News]] |access-date=May 29, 2024 }}</ref> She moved to Tianjin University in 2014, following her husband Jay S. Siegel, who became dean of Pharmaceutical Science and Technology at Tianjin in 2013.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/91/i43/American-Takes-Charge-Tianjin.html|magazine=Chemical & Engineering News|title=American Takes Charge In Tianjin|first=Jean-François|last=Tremblay|date=October 23, 2013|volume=91|issue=43}}</ref>

==Research==
Much of Baldridge's research involves finding better ways to use quantum mechanical methodologies to study complex molecules. For example, she used quantum mechanical approaches to study reaction paths and rates,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Baldridge |first1=Kim K. |last2=Gordon |first2=Mark S. |last3=Steckler |first3=Rozeanne |last4= Truhlar |first4=Donald G. |year=1989 |title=Ab initio reaction paths and direct dynamics calculations |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/j100350a018 |journal=[[The Journal of Physical Chemistry A|J. Phys. Chem.]] |volume=93 |issue=13 |pages=5107–5119 |doi=10.1021/j100350a018 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> inclusion of solvent effects,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Baldridge |first1=Kim |last2=Klamt |first2=Andreas |year=1997 |title=First principles implementation of solvent effects without outlying charge error  |url=https://pubs.aip.org/aip/jcp/article-abstract/106/16/6622/479415/First-principles-implementation-of-solvent-effects |journal=[[The Journal of Chemical Physics|J. Chem. Phys.]] |volume=106 |issue=16 |pages=6622–6633  |doi=10.1063/1.473662 |bibcode=1997JChPh.106.6622B |url-access=subscription }}</ref> and evaluation of [[Density functional theory|DFT]] functionals with [[London dispersion force|dispersion]] correction for studying large [[Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon|polynuclear aromatic molecules]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1= Peverati |first1=Roberto |last2=Baldridge |first2=Kim K |year=2008 |title=Implementation and Performance of DFT-D with Respect to Basis Set and Functional for Study of Dispersion Interactions in Nanoscale Aromatic Hydrocarbons |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ct800252z |journal=[[Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation|J. Chem. Theory Comput.]] |volume=4 |issue=12 |pages=2030–2048 |doi=10.1021/ct800252z |pmid=26620476 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Baldridge has contributed to quantum mechanical computer programs such as [[GAMESS (US)]], QMView, and GEMSTONE. GAMESS stands for General Atomic and Molecular Electronic System, and is an advanced chemistry program for calculations including generalized valence bond, the Hartree-Fock method, and density functional theory.<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jcc.540141112 |title=General atomic and molecular electronic structure system |last1=Schmidt |first1=Michael W. |last2=Baldridge |first2=Kim K. |last3=Boatz |first3=Jerry A. |last4=Elbert |first4=Steven T. |last5=Gordon |first5=Mark S. |last6=Jensen |first6=Jan H. |last7=Koseki |first7=Shiro |last8=Matsunaga |first8=Nikita |last9=Nguyen |first9=Kiet A. |last10=Su |first10=Shujun |last11=Windus |first11=Theresa L. |last12=Dupuis |first12=Michel |last13=Montgomery Jr |first13=John A. |journal=[[Journal of Computational Chemistry]] |year=1993 |volume=14 |issue=11 |pages=1347–1363 |doi=10.1002/jcc.540141112 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Awards and recognition==
Minot State University named Baldridge to their Academic Hall of Fame in 2013.<ref name=minot/> Baldridge is a [[Fellow of the American Physical Society]]<ref name=UCSD2001/> and was elected an [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] Chemistry Fellow in 2001.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.aaas.org/sites/default/files/AnnualReports/2001/fellows.pdf |title=Roster of Fellows for 2001 |website=www.aaas.org |access-date=May 30, 2024 }}</ref> She was given a 2019 Distinguished Women in Chemistry or Chemical Engineering Award by the [[International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry]] (IUPAC), the only winner from Asia.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://iupac.org/iupac-2019-distinguished-women/ |title=Awardees of the IUPAC 2019 Distinguished Women in Chemistry or Chemical Engineering |date=February 7, 2019 |website=iupac.org |access-date=May 29, 2024 }}</ref> The award was won for her work in developing and applying quantum chemistry programs in molecular science, for pioneering women-in-science symposia, and for championing for chemical safety in China.<ref name=cd>{{cite news|url=http://www.chinadaily.com.cn/edu/2019-03/27/content_37452494.htm|title=Tianjin University scientist awarded by IUPAC|date=March 27, 2019|newspaper=China Daily |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190905012302/http://www.chinadaily.com.cn/edu/2019-03/27/content_37452494.htm |archive-date=September 5, 2019}}</ref>
